title: Carbohydrates and lipids
introduction: Why does the same carbon chemistry make a soluble fuel, a tough wall and a self-assembling membrane?

sections.guidingQuestion: Why can carbon make a straight chain, a branch and a ring?
sections.explanation:
Carbon has four electrons available for covalent bonding. By sharing electrons with other non-metal atoms, one carbon atom can form four single bonds, or combinations including double bonds. Covalent bonds hold atoms together within a molecule.

Carbons can connect in unbranched chains, branched chains and single or multiple rings. The arrangement matters: a long hydrocarbon tail has different physical properties from a compact ring system. The same element can therefore support very different biological molecules.

Scientific conventions provide an internationally agreed language for recording dimensions. SI metric prefixes include kilo (10³), centi (10⁻²), milli (10⁻³), micro (10⁻⁶) and nano (10⁻⁹). These prefixes help biologists report the scale of molecules and cells consistently across laboratories; they are a nature-of-science convention, not another carbon bonding mechanism.
sections.revisionSummary: Carbon can make four covalent bonds; chains, branches, rings and double bonds produce structurally diverse molecules.
terms: Covalent bond: atoms share electron pairs
Carbon skeleton: arrangement of linked carbon atoms

sections.guidingQuestion: How can many small molecules become one macromolecule?
sections.explanation:
A monomer is a small unit that can link with similar units. In a condensation reaction, a new covalent link forms while the reacting groups release a small molecule, usually water, in the biological examples studied here.

Repeated links build polysaccharides from monosaccharides, polypeptides from amino acids and nucleic acids from nucleotides. The bond type differs between families; the shared pattern is that monomers become joined in a larger chain.

terms: Monomer: molecular building block
Polymer: molecule containing repeated linked units
Condensation: linking reaction that releases a small molecule

sections.guidingQuestion: How does digestion reverse the joining reaction?
sections.explanation:
In hydrolysis, water participates in breaking a covalent link. The water molecule supplies H to one product and OH to the other. This is the reverse type of chemical change to the condensation steps used in polymer building.

Digestive enzymes catalyse the hydrolysis of dietary polysaccharides and polypeptides into smaller molecules that can ultimately be absorbed. Adding water alone does not mean hydrolysis necessarily proceeds rapidly; enzymes support the reaction in biological conditions.

sections.guidingQuestion: What makes a small sugar suited for transport and energy release?
sections.explanation:
Monosaccharides are single sugars. In ring diagrams, pentoses contain five carbon atoms and hexoses contain six; count carbon atoms rather than simply counting corners, because a ring may include oxygen. Glucose is a hexose often represented as a six-membered ring.

Many hydroxyl groups make glucose water-soluble, so it can be transported in aqueous fluids. It is sufficiently stable for transport yet can be oxidized in cellular respiration to release usable energy. Its small size helps it move between transport and metabolic systems through suitable transport mechanisms.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why store glucose as a large branched polymer?
sections.explanation:
Starch stores alpha-glucose in plants; glycogen serves a corresponding role in animals. Coiling and branching make substantial stores comparatively compact. Glycogen is especially highly branched; starch includes unbranched amylose and branched amylopectin.

Large polymers are relatively insoluble, unlike freely dissolved glucose, limiting osmotic effects of accumulating large numbers of dissolved sugar molecules. Ends of chains are sites from which enzymes can add or remove alpha-glucose units, allowing stores to be mobilized.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why does a glucose polymer strengthen plant cell walls?
sections.explanation:
Cellulose links beta-glucose monomers with alternate residues oriented oppositely, producing long, relatively straight chains. The difference from alpha-glucose storage polysaccharides changes the three-dimensional arrangement.

Many parallel cellulose chains form hydrogen bonds with neighbouring chains. Bundles of microfibrils resist tensile forces in plant cell walls. Hydrogen bonds act between chains; the glucose units within each chain are held by covalent glycosidic bonds.

sections.guidingQuestion: How can a cell tell one surface from another?
sections.explanation:
Glycoproteins contain carbohydrate chains attached to proteins. On the outside of some cells, carbohydrate patterns form recognition labels. Cells and immune molecules can detect differences between these exposed surface structures.

ABO blood-group antigens involve distinct terminal carbohydrate structures on cell-surface glycoconjugates (including glycoproteins and glycolipids). A and B types differ in the sugar added to a shared precursor; type O does not add either A- or B-defining sugar. These identities matter for compatibility in transfusion.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why do oils separate from water?
sections.explanation:
Lipids include fats, oils, waxes and steroids. Many contain extensive non-polar C–C and C–H regions that do not interact favourably with polar water. They dissolve comparatively well in non-polar solvents but only sparingly in water.

Hydrophobic describes a region's interaction with water; it does not mean every atom in every lipid lacks polarity. Phospholipids have both hydrophobic tails and a hydrophilic head, an important distinction for membrane formation.

sections.guidingQuestion: How does changing one component create a different lipid function?
sections.explanation:
Glycerol has three hydroxyl-bearing positions that can react by condensation. A triglyceride has three fatty-acid chains joined to the glycerol backbone by ester bonds, with three water molecules released in this simplified overall formation.

In the syllabus model, a phospholipid links two fatty acids and a phosphate group to a glycerol scaffold. A phosphate-containing hydrophilic head and two hydrophobic hydrocarbon tails let it contribute to membranes instead of behaving like a neutral storage triglyceride. Some membrane phospholipids also carry other head-group attachments.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why are many oils liquid at room temperature?
sections.explanation:
A saturated fatty acid has no carbon-carbon double bonds in its chain; monounsaturated has one; polyunsaturated has more than one. The number and arrangement of C=C bonds affect shape and packing.

Common cis double bonds introduce bends, preventing adjacent fatty-acid chains from packing as closely as comparable saturated chains. This often lowers melting point; many plant oils contain more unsaturated fatty-acid chains, while fats used by endotherms for storage are often comparatively more saturated. Carbon-chain length and cis/trans geometry also matter, so double-bond count is not the only determinant.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why do many animals store triglycerides under the skin?
sections.explanation:
Triglycerides hold much chemical energy per unit mass and are hydrophobic, so they can be stored in droplets with comparatively little associated water. This suits long-term reserve storage better than free glucose.

Subcutaneous adipose tissue conducts heat relatively poorly compared with many water-rich tissues and can reduce heat transfer. The biological value depends on habitat, body size, thickness, circulation and temperature difference; insulation is not the same process as energy release in respiration.

misconceptions.correction: Stored fat can fuel respiration, but insulation reduces heat transfer through tissue.

sections.guidingQuestion: Which way will phospholipids turn in water?
sections.explanation:
A phospholipid is amphipathic: the phosphate-containing head is hydrophilic and interacts with water, whereas hydrocarbon tails are hydrophobic and avoid contact with surrounding water.

In an aqueous environment, phospholipids arrange so heads face the water on both sides while opposing tails point inward. This creates a continuous bilayer with a hydrophobic interior, a key structural feature of biological membranes. The real membrane also contains proteins and other lipids.

sections.guidingQuestion: How can some hormones enter cells without a transporter?
sections.explanation:
Steroids share a characteristic four-fused-carbon-ring framework (three six-membered and one five-membered ring), distinguishable from triglyceride fatty-acid tails and glucose rings. Oestradiol and testosterone are steroid hormones.

Their substantial non-polar regions can partition into the non-polar interior of phospholipid bilayers, allowing diffusion across membranes. Exact rates depend on the compound and membrane, but membrane permeability is not proof that the whole molecule lacks polar functional groups.

questions.prompt: A carbon atom in an organic molecule already forms one double bond and one single bond. How many additional single bonds can it usually make?

options.feedback: Two additional single bonds would make five bonding positions in total (2 + 1 + 2), exceeding the usual four.
Three additional single bonds would make six bonding positions in total. Carbon usually forms four in these neutral structures.
The current double plus single bond uses only three of the four positions, leaving one available.
A double bond uses two bonding positions and a single bond uses one: 4 − 2 − 1 = 1 remaining single bond.
